title: When a child dies
hookLine: the hardest grief; Christians hold it with Rachel weeping and with hope

cards: A small coffin is lighter than it should be. Nothing anyone says beside it makes it fit. This lesson goes slowly, and it's fine to stop at any point.
If this is your grief, nothing here is meant to explain it away. The Bible doesn't either. It gives a mother's voice, weeping in a town called Ramah, a voice that refuses to be comforted.
Christians have kept her voice in their scripture, and they hold this grief beside her.

teach.b: Her name is Rachel. In Genesis she is the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and she dies on the road. Later, the prophet Jeremiah hears her again, weeping over her people as they are carried away.

In the King James words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Refused to be comforted.
The Bible doesn't scold her. It writes it down.
Then Matthew's Gospel picks up the same line, after Herod has the little children of Bethlehem killed: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."
Right inside the Christmas story, a mother who cannot be consoled. Then a second thing.
In Jeremiah, God answers the weeping: "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD."

teach.h: THERE IS HOPE IN THINE END.
teach.b: And then, "there is hope in thine end." Weeping, then hope. Not hope instead of weeping.

teach.h: HE SHALL NOT RETURN TO ME.
teach.b: King David, when his infant son dies, says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Christian funeral prayers speak of the hope of the resurrection, and some Christians speak of seeing loved ones again.
Churches describe that hope in different ways, and some leave the details with God. Both voices stay in the book. The tears are not a failure of faith.
In the Bible, they are part of it.

how: Christians mourn children with funerals, prayers and the hope of the resurrection; churches hold services of remembrance, some offer support groups for bereaved parents, and traditions differ in how they speak about children who die.

games.q: what does “when a child dies” mean?
o: a grief the Bible lets weep, with hope set right beside it
a loss the Bible says faith should help you quickly get over
a sorrow the Bible keeps out of the Christmas story

games.q: when a child dies — tap the pairs.
p: weeping for her children in Ramah
what the text says, without scolding
there is hope in thine end

s: the Bible tells Rachel to stop crying because grief shows weak faith
the text writes down that she refused to be comforted, and doesn't scold her.
Matthew's Gospel quotes Rachel's weeping in the Christmas story
after Herod has the little children of Bethlehem killed.
in Jeremiah, hope replaces the weeping as if it never happened
the weeping is recorded first, and the hope is spoken beside it.

games.q: you're one of King David's servants. while his infant son was sick, David fasted and lay on the ground. now the child has died, and you're afraid to tell him. when he finds out, what does David do?
o: he tears his clothes and refuses food for many more days.
he gets up, washes, worships, and eats.
he blames his servants and sends them away.
games.why: David rises, washes, goes to worship, then eats. his servants are confused, and he says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

practice: If you know a mother or father who has lost a child, at any age, bring their face to mind; if not, hold the ones you'll never meet, in a hospital tonight or a town at war.
Stay with them without reaching for words, the way someone sits beside a person who is crying, and if you pray, simply say Rachel's name and let God fill in the rest.
If this grief is your own and it feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: When a child dies. The grief the Bible gives to Rachel, who would not be comforted, and the hope held beside it, without taking her tears away.

orig.note: Hebrew: Rachel, the mother whose weeping Jeremiah hears in Ramah.

carryVoice: Your line: rachel weeping. Her tears stay in the book, beside the hope. Back tomorrow, same hill.
